statement: Divide the "generation" and "retail" aspects of power companies

summary.why: This party says that New Zealanders are paying too much for power, because four large companies generate 90 percent of NZ's power, controlling the supply and selling the power directly to customers. The party says that this situation results in high prices for households and industry, leading to companies closing down and job losses.
summary.how: This party would replace the current system so that generation and retail are not done by the same companies. This would make sure that the most expensive generator would not set the price for the rest of the market.

statement: Guarantee fixed-price contracts for new electricity generation projects

summary.why: This party says that prices for electricity are too high in NZ. Because of the structure of the market with four major companies, it is hard for competitors to enter the market. The "gentailer" companies can hold back supply, making electricity more expensive, instead of investing in more power generation.
summary.how: This party would guarantee long-term, fixed-price contractions for building new electricity generation. The companies building this infrastructure would receive guarantees that their power would be the first to be used when needed. This would make it easier for investors to fund electricity generation projects, and increase New Zealand's energy security and resilience.

statement: Separate the Foodstuffs supermarket chain into two national cooperatives

summary.why: This party says that food prices are too high in New Zealand, as a result of a supermarket duopoly controlling 80% of the grocery market. Food producers and households do not get a good deal from this system. Creating more competition will drive prices down.
summary.how: This party would introduce legislation to split the Foodstuffs brands into two cooperatives; one for New World and Four Square and the other for Pak'n'Save. This would create more competition with Woolworths and result in lower prices and fairer deals for producers. This would create more certainty for major businesses like McCains and Heinz Watties, which have experienced job losses as a result of a poorly functioning system.

statement: Give the Commerce Commission and Grocery Commissioner more powers

summary.why: This party says that the current Grocery Commissioner does not have the power to enforce the sector properly. The Commerce Commission cannot apply penalties as high as its counterpoint in Australia, investigations are often slow, and penalties are not enforced.
summary.how: This party would increase the powers assigned to the Commerce Commission and Grocery Commissioner. The Commerce Commission would be able to apply penalties for serious breaches of up to $10 million, three times the gain, or 10 percent of turnover. Investigations would be faster and enforcement stricter. The Grocery Commissioner would have powers to investigate, make binding decisions and apply penalties directly.

summary.why: This party says that prices for food are too high in NZ, in part because supermarkets limit small food providers' access to customers. The supermarkets control suppliers' access to the market, favouring larger providers.
summary.how: This party would introduce a new industry framework into the Commerce Act 1986 to fix competition issues quickly without waiting for legislative change. This would ensure producers are not pushed off supermarket shelves by larger players.

statement: Return at least 50 percent of mining project royalties to the region where mining took place

summary.why: This party says that mining plays a vital role in NZ's economy and regions as one of the country's most productive sectors. The benefits of mining do not always stay in these regions, and communities should directly benefit from local mining projects. If mining expands, infrastructure and development in the regions must grow too.
summary.how: This party would invest 50 percent of mining royalties in the region the resources were extracted from. This money would be spend on infrastructure like flood protection, energy generation transport and housing development and would be backed up by targeted regional investment. This money would also fund Mines Rescue capabilities.

summary.why: This party says that New Zealand's birth rate is only 1.53 children per woman, when the replacement rate is 2.1 children per woman. If something is not done, this party says New Zealand may become entirely dependent on immigration in the future.

statement: Increase the milk quantity guaranteed to NZ dairy manufacturing

summary.why:
This party says that the present 50 million litres per year is too low to incentivise production at a large scale. The status-quo supports New Zealand-based dairy manufacturers, but does not support these firms to scale to size, which disincentives investment into Fonterra. 

Marketing ‘New Zealand Dairy’, this party sees this policy as a means of making NZ’s dairy manufacturing sector more competitive in export markets. It says it is important for the milk provision not to be a subsidy; dairy manufacturing firms would cover delivery and collection costs and pay farmers market rates.
summary.how: This party would increase milk access from 50 million litres to 500 million litres per year over the first six years. From there, access would taper to 80 per cent, 60 per cent, 40 per cent and 20 per cent to encourage immediate investment. This would be done through changing the Dairy Industry Restructuring Act 2001.

statement: Establish a Special Economic Zone at Marsden Point

summary.why: This party says Marsden Point should be allowed to operate under a lighter regulatory framework to support domestic energy production. The party argues that, with rising global tensions and increasing energy costs, New Zealand needs to better ensure itself against spikes in global fuel prices. Establishing a special economic zone (SEZ) will attract foreign investment.
summary.how: This party would establish a Special Economic Zone, which would see a combination of tax breaks, wage subsidies, and reduced regulation to incentivise the development of energy and port operations. The party says that the principal benefits of the economic zone would be the bypassing of planning regulations and the RMA. If elected, this party would consider providing additional funding to help local councils run services in the SEZ, such as investment in physical, transport or communications infrastructure.

statement: Introduce a binding referendum on the Māori seats

summary.why: This party says that Māori have been better represented since the establishment of MMP. When MMP was introduced, a report recommended scrapping the old Māori seats because Māori would be better represented. The party argues that a referendum is needed to justify the seats' existence and so the issue can be settled. It also cites the conduct of Te Pati Māori in Parliament as justifying the need for a referendum.

It says the referendum would have no extra costs if it could be included on the ballot papers at the next general election. The result would not affect the outcomes of that election, but the following election three years later.

statement: Ensure that only NZ citizens can vote

summary.why: This party says that it is a problem that after two years of living in NZ, someone can claim permanent residency and vote. For visa holders who have no expiry date for their visa, they can technically vote after one year. It says that only those who are natural-born citizens and have sworn allegiance to NZ should be able to vote for who governs the country and in referendums that can change NZ.
summary.how:
This party would restrict voting rights for all referenda and levels of government (including local government) to those with legal citizenship.

Permanent residents will still retain other rights such as the right to live, work, study, and access government support.

statement: Allow a two-year amnesty on overstayers if they self-deport

summary.why: This party says that the illegal overstaying of visas by migrants is causing public distrust of the immigration system. However, people have built a life here and are discouraged by bans on re-entering the country if caught and deported.
summary.how: This party would provide a 24-month/two-year amnesty whereby, if one chooses to self-deport by leaving the country, they will be eligible to apply to immigrate to NZ legally. statement: Remove automatic work rights from student visas

summary.why: This party says that student visa holders compete in the competitive graduate job market and can take jobs from New Zealanders. It stays the intent of international education is for overseas economies to give money to NZ by paying for their education, not to provide automatic work rights and residence pathways. The party also cites broader concern with net numbers of migrants entering New Zealand and sees changes to student visas as a way of reducing net migration and its effect on infrastructure.
summary.how: This party would have student visa holders lose their automatic right to work. To be allowed to work, student visa holders would have to fulfil strict conditions to ensure they are not doing work that could be done by NZ citizens. People who have been on student visas and want to transition to another visa would have to leave NZ and reapply for a new visa from overseas.

statement: Promote healthy eating as preventative healthcare

summary.why: This party says that too large a share of NZ health spending goes towards caring for people once they're sick, as opposed to before. The party claims that 59% of health spending is spent treating chronic illness, and only 1.75% on the prevention of such conditions.
summary.how: This party would promote nutrition from primary school to medical school, use health coaches in GP care, and require a full independent review of our dietary guidelines. It would fund research and development to better assess nutritional interventions for preventing and treating mental illness. It would fund development in agricultural tech and cut regulatory barriers to help grow markets for organic food items.  It would investigate how the use of vitamins in the delivery of healthcare can prevent people from getting sick again, including intravenous vitamin C pre- and post-surgery for preventing and treating infections.

The party cites the additional, but temporary, $50 added to the IWFTC by the government this year as needing to be increased and made permanent. summary.how: This party would increase the IWFTC by $70 a week. The increase would not apply to the Family Tax Credit (FTC), which covers parents regardless of employment status. This party estimates that this policy would cost between $500m and $600m annually.

statement: Replace the Accredited Employer Work Visa with a shortage-led skilled work visa

summary.why: This party says that NZ's immigration system should be used to manage genuine workforce shortages.  However, it says that instead the accredited employer work visa has too often been used as a means to simply find a preferable candidate and is a risk for the workers themselves, who can find themselves with less protection from exploitation.
summary.how: This party would replace the Accredited Employer Work Visa with the shortage-led skilled work visa. Such a visa would be limited to shortages, requiring evidence of attempted NZ recruitment, transparency data, and a wage floor to protect domestic wages. The party also says the reforms should be targeted towards the most needed industries, which would restrict access for other industries that have a larger domestic workforce.

statement: Increase the funding for the NZ Coastguard

summary.why: This party says that Coastguard, as an organisation, is funded only 40% by the government. 60% of its funding comes from public donations. The party argues that an essential service needs a more reliable funding model, so the organisation has greater certainty.

statement: Establish a combat sport commission
